name_en: Trà Shan Tuyết Cổ Thụ (Ancient Tree Snow Shan)
aliases: Trà Shan Tuyết Cổ Thụ (Snow Shan Tea)
processing: Made from old mountain tea trees; most often as green tea, with white and other styles also made by some producers.
harvest_season: Spring buds are usually the most sought after, as with other high-mountain tree teas; picking continues in later seasons at lower prices.
appearance_dry: Long, twisted leaves, often with visible pale down on the buds.
appearance_wet: Large, thick leaves from tall old trees.
taste_profile: Mild astringency that turns into a deep, lasting sweetness, with honey and mountain-herb aromas reported from the best-known areas.

brewing.notes: Sturdy large leaf takes hotter water than a Chinese spring green, and repays many short gongfu steeps.

vintage_note: Usually sold by the year's harvest and by spring picking, though small producers may not date it clearly. Fresh green lots are best within a year or so; white lots from the same trees may be kept longer. Age of tree is a selling claim that is hard to check, so buy from makers who name a commune.
description:
Shan Tuyết means something like snowy mountain, after the pale down on the buds. These are the tall old tea trees of Vietnam's northern mountains, native to the area and closely tied to Dao and Hmong communities. Hà Giang is the province most associated with them, though Sơn La and Yên Bái have them as well.

The leaf is usually made as a green tea, though white teas and other styles are also produced from it. The big thick leaf gives a far heavier body than most lowland greens.

The typical description is a soft bitterness that quickly turns sweet and stays in the throat, with honey and herbs in the aroma. Treat it more like a Yunnan tree tea than a delicate green: hot water, short steeps, many rounds.

Cổ thụ means ancient tree, and that is a claim worth questioning. Tea from these communes is not automatically from old trees, and much is sold from younger plantings. Ask which commune and maker it comes from, and expect to pay more for real old-tree buds.
history:
The age of these trees is a local boast with some support: Vietnamese reports describe trees in Hà Giang as well over 200 years old, and some as over three centuries, though exact ages are rarely measured.

Formal recognition came recently. Hà Giang's shan tuyết tea received a geographical indication covering 44 communes, and in 2019 another 1,324 trees in the province were listed as Vietnamese Heritage Trees, bringing its total to 1,629.
